terms.latin: agō cum aliquō dē aliquā rē
terms.gloss: treat with someone about something, negotiate
terms.grammar: verb phrase: agō, agere, ēgī, āctum
evidence: Caes. BG 1.13.3: Is ita cum Caesare ēgit
Traupman 187: agere cum aliquō dē pāce, to have peace negotiations with someone
terms.comment: The plain classical way to say it (Lewis & Short s.v. agō): to negotiate peace, dē pāce agere; to put forward terms, condiciōnēs ferre (see propose). The talks themselves are colloquium (see negotiation).

terms.gloss: bargain, settle terms, make a deal
evidence: Plin. Ep. 3.12.1: sed jam nunc pacīscor
terms.comment: To bargain and come to terms (with long ī, de Vaan 452; see haggle, agreement); the deal made is pactum.

Classically to carry business through to the end, to settle it: what one does once the negotiating is over; cum aliquō trānsigere, to come to a settlement with someone (Lewis & Short). M-O gives it for negotiating itself. Its other sense is to run through with a weapon (poetry and later prose).

phrases.latin: Is ita cum Caesare ēgit: sī pācem populus Rōmānus cum Helvētiīs faceret, in eam partem itūrōs atque ibi futūrōs Helvētiōs ubi eōs Caesar cōnstituisset atque esse voluisset
phrases.english: He negotiated with Caesar as follows: if the Roman people made peace with the Helvetii, they would go and stay wherever Caesar settled them and wished them to be

phrases.latin: veniam ad cēnam, sed jam nunc pacīscor, sit expedīta sit parca
phrases.english: I’ll come to dinner, but I’m setting my terms now: let it be quick, let it be frugal

sources: Lewis & Short: ago · Lewis & Short: paciscor · Lewis & Short: transigo
